metadata.title: A Note on Spectral Analysis in automorphic representation theory for $\GL_2$: II

nodes.name: Singular case
nodes.statement: However, neither \cite{Za82} nor \cite[\S 4.3]{MV10} was capable of explicitly treating an exceptional case (we shall call it the \emph{singular case}), in which $\varphi$ has the quasi-character $\norm_{\ag{A}}$ in its set of exponents \cite[\S 4.3.3]{MV10}.
nodes.statement_short: The exceptional case where the quasi-character $\norm_{\ag{A}}$ lies in the exponent set of $\varphi$.
differentia: $\varphi$ has the quasi-character $\norm_{\ag{A}}$ in its set of exponents

nodes.name: Regularized integral via subtraction of the non integral part
nodes.statement: (1) We subtract from $\varphi$ a non integral part $\Reis(\varphi)$, considered to have integral $0$ by abuse of orthogonality, and define $$ \int^{\reg} \varphi = \int \varphi - \Reis(\varphi). $$
differentia: We subtract from $\varphi$ a non integral part $\Reis(\varphi)$

nodes.name: Regularized integral via residue of $\int \varphi \cdot E(s)$
nodes.statement: (2) We introduced some suitable meromorphic function $E(s)$ with constant residue $1$ at $0$, such that $$ \int \varphi \cdot E(s) $$ is convergent for certain range of $s$ and has a meromorphic continuation. We then define $$ \int^{\reg} \varphi = \Res_{s=0} \int \varphi \cdot E(s). $$
nodes.statement_short: Define the regularized integral as the residue at $s=0$ of the meromorphically continued $\int \varphi \cdot E(s)$.

nodes.name: Regularized integral via a measure-operator $\sigma_0$
nodes.statement: (3) We find a/any measure-operator $\sigma_0$ such that the convolution $\sigma_0 * \varphi$ becomes integrable, and that the dual measure $\sigma_0^{\vee}$ with respect to change of variables satisfies $\sigma_0^{\vee} * 1 = R_0 \neq 0$. We then define $$ \int^{\reg} \varphi = R_0^{-1} \int \sigma_0 * \varphi. $$
nodes.statement_short: Define the regularized integral by convolving with a measure $\sigma_0$ that makes $\varphi$ integrable, then normalizing by $R_0$.

nodes.name: Definition 2.1 (regularizable function on $\ag{R}_+$)
nodes.statement: Let $a: \ag{R}_+ \to \ag{C}$ be a continuous function. It is \emph{regularizable} if \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] for any $N \gg 1$ as $t \to \infty$ $$ a(t) = f(t)+O(t^{-N}), \quad f(t)=\sum_{i=1}^l \frac{c_i}{n_i!} t^{\frac{1}{2}+\alpha_i} \log^{n_i}t, $$ where $c_i, \alpha_i \in \ag{C}, n_i \in \ag{N}$; \item[(2)] for some $\alpha \in \ag{R}$ as $t \to 0^+$ $$ a(t) = O(t^{\alpha}). $$ \end{itemize} In this case, we write for $T > 0$ $$ h_T(s) = \sum_{i=1}^l \frac{c_i}{n_i!} \frac{\partial^{n_i}}{\partial s^{n_i}} \left( \frac{T^{s+\alpha_i}}{s+\alpha_i} \right) = \sum_{i=1}^l c_i \sum_{m=0}^{n_i} \frac{(-1)^{n_i-m}}{m!} \frac{T^{s+\alpha_i} \log^m T}{(s+\alpha_i)^{n_i-m+1}}. $$
nodes.statement_short: A continuous $a$ on $\ag{R}_+$ is regularizable when it matches a finite sum $f(t)=\sum c_i t^{1/2+\alpha_i}\log^{n_i}t$ up to $O(t^{-N})$ at $\infty$ and is $O(t^{\alpha})$ at $0^+$; $h_T(s)$ is the associated antiderivative-type sum.

nodes.name: Closure $\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}}$ of a one parameter subgroup in $\ag{T}^n$
nodes.statement: \noindent Write $\ag{T} = \ag{R} / \ag{Z}$. Let $\vec{\theta} = (\theta_1, \cdots, \theta_n) \in \ag{R}^n$. For any $\vec{x} \in \ag{R}^n$, we write by $[\vec{x}]$ its image in $\ag{T}^n$. Define $$ \ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}} = \overline{\lbrace [t\vec{\theta}] : t\in \ag{R} \rbrace}. $$ It is a closed subgroup of $\ag{T}^n$. Furthermore, the one parameter subgroup $U_{\vec{\theta}} = \lbrace t.\vec{\theta} : t \in \ag{R} \rbrace$ of $\ag{R}^n$ acts uniquely ergodically on $\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}}$ w.r.t. the Haar measure of $\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}}$ is the closure of the line $\{[t\vec{\theta}]\}$ in $\ag{T}^n=(\ag{R}/\ag{Z})^n$, on which $U_{\vec{\theta}}$ acts uniquely ergodically.

nodes.name: Definition 2.5 (slowly increasing function)
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi: \GL_2(\F)\gp{Z}(\ag{A}) \backslash \GL_2(\ag{A}) \to \ag{C}$ be a continuous function. It is \emph{slowly increasing} if for some $c \in \ag{R}$ and $g$ lying in some Siegel domain we have $$ \norm[\varphi(g)] \ll \Ht(g)^c, \Ht(g) \to \infty. $$

nodes.name: Definition 2.6 (regularizing kernel $a(t,\varphi)$)
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi: \GL_2(\F)\gp{Z}(\ag{A}) \backslash \GL_2(\ag{A}) \to \ag{C}$ be a slowly increasing function. Its \emph{regularizing kernel} $a(t,\varphi)$ is $$ a(t,\varphi) = \int_{\F \backslash \ag{A} \times \F^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{(1)} \times \gp{K}} \varphi(n(x)a(t^+y)k) dx d^{\times}y dk, $$ where $t^+ = s_{\F}(t)$ is the image of $t$ under the section of the adelic norm map $\ag{A}^{\times} \to \ag{R}_+$ recalled in the beginning of this paper.
nodes.statement_short: The regularizing kernel of $\varphi$ is its average over $\gp{N}\times\ag{A}^{(1)}\times\gp{K}$ at height $t$.

nodes.name: Definition 2.7 (regularizable function on $\GL_2$, $R(s,\varphi)$ and $\Aut^{\reg}(\GL_2)$)
nodes.statement: We call a slowly increasing function $\varphi: \GL_2(\F)\gp{Z}(\ag{A}) \backslash \GL_2(\ag{A}) \to \ag{C}$ \emph{regularizable} if its regularizing kernel $a(t,\varphi)$ satisfies the condition (1) of Definition \ref{RegFuncRDef}. In this case, we define for $s \in \ag{C}, \Re s \gg 1$ $$ R(s,\varphi) = \int_0^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t)) t^{s-\frac{1}{2}} \frac{dt}{t}; \quad R^*(s,\varphi) = \Lambda_{\F}(1+2s) R(s,\varphi). $$ The space of regularizable functions is denoted by $\Aut^{\reg}(\GL_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi$ is regularizable if its regularizing kernel satisfies the asymptotic condition (1), and then $R(s,\varphi)$ is the Mellin transform of $a(t,\varphi)-f(t)$.
differentia: its regularizing kernel $a(t,\varphi)$ satisfies the condition (1) of Definition

nodes.name: Definition 2.12 (regularized integral, principal part and degenerate part)
nodes.statement: We define the \emph{regularized integral} of a regularizable function $\varphi: [\PGL_2] \to \ag{C}$ as $$ \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \varphi(g) dg = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \left( \Res_{s=\frac{1}{2}} R(s,\varphi) + c_i \delta_{\substack{\alpha_i=-\frac{1}{2} \\ n_i=0}} \right), $$ where $c_i, \alpha_i, n_i$ are associated with $a(t,\varphi)$ as in Definition \ref{RegFuncRDef}. We call the first term the \emph{principal part} of the regularized integral, the second the \emph{degenerate part} of the regularized integral. The regularized integral is linear and extends the integral on $\Aut^{\reg}(\GL_2) \cap \intL^1(\GL_2, 1)$.
nodes.statement_short: The regularized integral of $\varphi$ is $\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)^{-1}$ times the residue of $R(s,\varphi)$ at $s=1/2$ plus a degenerate term.

Let $\omega$ be a unitary character of $\F^{	imes}  ackslash \ag{A}^{	imes}$. Let $\varphi$ be a smooth function on $\GL_2(\F)  ackslash \GL_2(\ag{A})$ with central character $\omega$. We call $\varphi$ \emph{finitely regularizable} if there exist characters $\chi_i: \F^{	imes}  ackslash \ag{A}^{	imes} 	o \ag{C}^{(1)}$, $\alpha_i \in \ag{C}, n_i \in \ag{N}$ and smooth functions $f_i \in \Ind_{\gp{B}(\ag{A}) \cap \gp{K}}^{\gp{K}} (\chi_i, \omega \chi_i^{-1})$ for $1 \leq i \leq l$, such that for any $M \gg 1$ $$ \varphi(n(x)a(y)k) = \varphi_{\gp{N}}^*(n(x)a(y)k) + O(
orm[y]_{\ag{A}}^{-M}), 	ext{ as }

orm[y]_{\ag{A}}^{ rac{1}{2}+\alpha_i} \log^{n_i} 
orm[y]_{\ag{A}} f_i(k). $$ In this case, we call $\Ex(\varphi)=\{ \chi_i

nodes.name: Definition 2.15 (regularizing Eisenstein series $\Eis^{\reg}(s,f)$)
nodes.statement: In the case $\omega^{-1}\xi^2(t)=\norm[t]_{\ag{A}}^{i\mu}$ for some $\mu \in \ag{R}$, we introduce the \emph{regularizing Eisenstein series} for $f \in V_{\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}}^{\infty}$ and $s$ in a neighborhood of $(1-i\mu)/2$ $$ \Eis^{\reg}(s,f)(g) = \Eis(s,f)(g) - \frac{\Lambda_{\F}(1-2s-i\mu)}{\Lambda_{\F}(1+2s+i\mu)} \int_{\gp{K}} f(\kappa) d\kappa \cdot \chi^{-1}(\det g) \norm[\det g]_{\ag{A}}^{\frac{i\mu}{2}}. $$ It is holomorphic at $s=(1-i\mu)/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Subtract from $\Eis(s,f)$ the polar multiple of a quasi-character so that the result is holomorphic at $s=(1-i\mu)/2$.

nodes.name: Definition 2.19 ($\intL^2$-residual space $\Reis(\GL_2,\omega)$)
nodes.statement: Let $\omega$ be a unitary character of $\F^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{\times}$. The $\intL^2$-\emph{residual space} of central character $\omega$, denoted by $\Reis(\GL_2,\omega)$, is the direct sum of the vector spaces $\Reis^+(\GL_2,\omega)$ resp. $\Reis^{\reg}(\GL_2,\omega)$ spanned by functions $$ \frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} \Eis(s,f), \text{if } s \neq \frac{1-i\mu}{2} \quad \text{resp.} \quad \frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} \Eis^{\reg}(\frac{1-i\mu}{2},f) $$ where $s \in \ag{C}, \Re s > 0$ and for some unitary character $\xi$ of $\F^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{\times}$, $f \in V_{\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}}^{\infty}$ and $\mu$ as above.
nodes.statement_short: The residual space is spanned by $s$-derivatives of ordinary Eisenstein series and, at the singular point, of regularizing Eisenstein series.
nodes.genus: the direct sum of the vector spaces $\Reis^+(\GL_2,\omega)$ resp. $\Reis^{\reg}(\GL_2,\omega)$

nodes.name: Definition 2.25 ($\intL^2$-residue $\Reis(\varphi)$)
nodes.statement: In the case (2), we call $\Reis(\varphi)$ the $\intL^2$-residue of $\varphi$. For definiteness, we shall write $\Reis(\varphi)$ to be the one given by (\ref{ReisDef}).

nodes.name: Definition 3.2 (intertwining operator $\Intw_s$ and its regularized variant $\widetilde{\Intw}_s$)
nodes.statement: If $f \in \Res_{\gp{K}}^{\GL_2(\ag{A})} \pi(\xi_1,\xi_2)$, we define for any $s \in \ag{C}$ an operator $\Intw_s: \Res_{\gp{K}}^{\GL_2(\ag{A})} \pi(\xi_1,\xi_2) \to \Res_{\gp{K}}^{\GL_2(\ag{A})} \pi(\xi_2,\xi_1)$ (abuse of notations) by requiring $$ \Intw_s f_s(a(y)\kappa) = \xi_2(y)\norm[y]_{\ag{A}}^{\frac{1}{2}-s} \Intw_sf(\kappa), \quad \text{i.e.,} \quad \Intw_s f_s = (\Intw_s f)_{-s}; $$ $$ \text{resp.} \quad \widetilde{\Intw}_s = \Intw_s \circ (I-\ProjP_{\gp{K}}e_{\xi}), \quad \text{if } \xi_1=\xi_2=\xi $$ with the Taylor expansion at $s=0$ resp. $s=1/2$ when $\xi_1=\xi_2 = \xi$ (since $\Intw_s$ is ``diagonalizable'') $$ \Intw_sf = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{s^n}{n!} \Intw_0^{(n)}f, \quad \text{resp.} \quad \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2+s} f = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{s^n}{n!} \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2}^{(n)}f. $$ Here $\ProjP_{\gp{K}}$, with $d\kappa$ the probability Haar measure on $\gp{K}$, is defined to be the map $$ \pi(\xi,\xi) \to \ag{C}, f \mapsto \int_{\gp{K}} f(\kappa) \xi^{-1}(\kappa) d\kappa, $$ and $e_{\xi} = \xi \circ \det \in \Res_{\gp{K}}^{\GL_2(\ag{A})} \pi(\xi,\xi)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Intw_s$ is normalized so that $\Intw_s f_s=(\Intw_s f)_{-s}$, with Taylor expansion at $s=0$ (resp. $s=1/2$ after removing the $\gp{K}$-projection $\ProjP_{\gp{K}}$ when $\xi_1=\xi_2$).

nodes.name: Constant term $\eisCst(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)$ of the Eisenstein series
nodes.statement: $$ \Eis(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f) = \eisCst(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f) + \left( \Eis(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f) - \eisCst(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f) \right) \text{ with} $$ $$ \eisCst(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)(g) := \int_{\F \backslash \ag{A}} \Eis(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)(n(x)g) dx, n(x) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x \\ & 1 \end{pmatrix} $$ and study the growth in $g$ of $\eisCst(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)$ and $\Eis(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f) - \eisCst(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)$ separately, as well as all their derivatives with respect to $s$.
nodes.statement_short: Split $\Eis$ into its constant term along $\gp{N}$ and the remainder, and study the growth of each separately.

nodes.name: Whittaker function $W(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)$
nodes.statement: $$ \Eis(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)(g) - \eisCst(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)(g) = \sum_{\alpha \in \F^{\times}} W(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)(a(\alpha)g) \text{ with } a(\alpha)=\begin{pmatrix} \alpha & \\ & 1 \end{pmatrix} $$ $$ \text{and} \quad W(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)(g) = \int_{\F \backslash \ag{A}} \psi(-x) \Eis(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)(n(x)g) dx, $$ where $\psi$ is the standard additive character of $\F \backslash \ag{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: The non-constant part of $\Eis$ is the sum over $\alpha \in \F^{\times}$ of the $\psi$-Whittaker coefficient $W(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)$.

nodes.name: Non flat section $f_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};g)$ attached to a Schwartz function
nodes.statement: If $\Phi \in \Sch(\ag{A}^2)$ is a Schwartz function, we can define the following (non flat) section in $V_{s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}}^{\infty}$ $$ f_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};g) = \xi(\det g)\norm[\det g]_{\ag{A}}^{\frac{1}{2}+s} \int_{\ag{A}^{\times}} \Phi((0,t)g) \omega^{-1}\xi^2(t) \norm[t]_{\ag{A}}^{1+2s} d^{\times}t $$ first defined for $\Re s > 0$ then meromorphically continued to $s \in \ag{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: A Schwartz function $\Phi$ on $\ag{A}^2$ produces a (non flat) section by a zeta-type integral over $\ag{A}^{\times}$.

nodes.name: Definition 5.5 (Schwartz semi-norms $\Sch_l^{\vec{p},\vec{m}}$ on $\Sch(\ag{R}^d)$)
nodes.statement: For $l \in [1,\infty]$, $\vec{p}, \vec{m} \in \ag{N}^d$, we put the semi-norm $\Sch_l^{\vec{p},\vec{m}}$ on $\Sch(\ag{R}^d)$ by $$ \Sch_l^{\vec{p},\vec{m}}(\Phi) = \extNorm{ \vec{x}^{\vec{p}} \cdot \partial^{\vec{m}} \Phi }_l. $$ Here we have written: \begin{itemize} \item $\Norm_l$ is the $\intL^l$-norm on $\ag{R}^d$. \item For $\vec{x}=(x_i)_{1 \leq i \leq d} \in \ag{R}^d, \vec{p}=(p_i)_{1 \leq i \leq d} \in \ag{N}^d$, $\vec{x}^{\vec{p}}=\Pi_{i=1}^d x_i^{p_i}$. \item For $\vec{n}=(n_i)_{1 \leq i \leq d} \in \ag{N}^d, \vec{x}=(x_i)_{1 \leq i \leq d} \in \ag{R}^d$, $$ \partial^{\vec{n}} = \prod_{i=1}^d \frac{\partial^{n_i}}{\partial x_i^{n_i}}. $$ \end{itemize}

nodes.name: The spaces $\fsB_c(\ag{R}_+)$ and $\fsH_c(\ag{C})$
nodes.statement: For any $c \in \ag{R}$, define $$ \fsB_c(\ag{R}_+) = \left\{ f: \in \Cont^{\infty}(\ag{R}_+): \sup_{y > 0} \norm[f^{(k)}(y) y^{\sigma+k}] < \infty, \forall \sigma > c \right\}. $$ $$ \fsH_c(\ag{C}) = \left\{ M \text{ holomorphic in } \Re s > c: \sup_{\Re s = \sigma} \norm[s(s+1)\cdots (s+k-1)M(s)] < \infty, \forall \sigma > c \right\}. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\fsB_c(\ag{R}_+)$ consists of smooth functions with controlled decay $y^{\sigma+k}$, and $\fsH_c(\ag{C})$ of holomorphic functions with polynomially controlled vertical growth.

Definition 5.14 (Fourier decomposition $f_{\xi}$ along $\F^1$)
nodes.statement: We write the multiplicative group $\F^1 = \{ x \in \F: \norm[x]_{\F} = 1 \}$. For any function $f$ on $\F^{\times}$ and any character $\xi \in \widehat{\F^1}$ we define a function on $\ag{R}_+$ $$ f_{\xi}(t) = f(t;\xi) = \int_{\F^1} f(tu) \xi(u) du, t > 0 $$ where $du$ is the probability Haar measure on $\F^1$. Concretely: \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] If $\F=\ag{R}$ then $\F^1=\{ \pm 1\}, \widehat{\F^1}=\{ \xi_+, \xi_- \}$ with $\xi_+ \equiv 1$ and $\xi_-(-1)=-1$. We then define $$ f(t;+) = f_+(t) = \frac{1}{2} \left( f(t) + f(-t) \right), f(t;-) = f_-(t) = \frac{1}{2} \left( f(t) - f(-t) \right). $$ \item[(2)] If $\F=\ag{C}$ then $\F^1=\{ e^{i \theta}: \theta \in \ag{R}/2\pi \ag{Z} \}, \widehat{\F^1}=\{ \xi_n: n \in \ag{Z} \}$ with $\xi_n(e^{i\theta}) = e^{i n \theta}$. We then define $$ f(t;n) = f_n(t) = \int_{\ag{R} / 2\pi \ag{Z}} f(te^{i\theta}) e^{in\theta} \frac{d\theta}{2\pi}. $$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Project a function on $\F^{\times}$ onto the $\xi$-isotypic part along the norm-one subgroup $\F^1$, explicitly $f_{\pm}$ for $\F=\ag{R}$ and $f_n$ for $\F=\ag{C}$.

nodes.name: Definition 5.16 (support index, additive and multiplicative invariance indices)
nodes.statement: Let $d \geq 1$ be an integer. For any $\Phi \in \Sch(\F^d)$ we define its \emph{support index} $D(\Phi) \in \ag{Z}$, \emph{additive invariance index} $\delta(\Phi) \in \ag{Z}$ and \emph{multiplicative invariance index} $m(\Phi) \in \ag{N}$ as follows. \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] $D(\Phi)$ is the largest integer $D$ such that $$ \Phi(\vec{x}) \neq 0 \Rightarrow \vec{x} \in \vp^D \times \cdots \times \vp^D. $$ \item[(2)] $\delta(\Phi)$ is the smallest integer $\delta$ such that $$ \Phi(\vec{x}+\vec{t}) = \Phi(\vec{x}), \forall \vec{x} \in \F^d, \vec{t} \in \vp^{\delta} \times \cdots \times \vp^{\delta}. $$ \item[(3)] $m(\Phi)$ is the smallest integer $m \geq 0$ such that for any $\kappa \in \GL_d(\vo)$ with $\kappa-1 \in \Mat_d(\vp^m)$ $$ \rpR(\kappa).\Phi(\vec{x}) = \Phi(\vec{x}.\kappa) = \Phi(\vec{x}), \forall \vec{x} \in \F^d. $$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: For $\Phi \in \Sch(\F^d)$: $D(\Phi)$ measures the support, $\delta(\Phi)$ the additive invariance, $m(\Phi)$ the invariance under congruence subgroups of $\GL_d(\vo)$.

nodes.name: Definition 5.18 (semi-norms $\Sch_l^{\vec{\sigma}}$ on $\Sch(\F^d)$)
nodes.statement:
For $l \in [1,\infty]$, $\vec{\sigma} \in \ag{R}_{\geq 0}^d$, we put the semi-norm $\Sch_l^{\vec{\sigma}}$ on $\Sch(\F^d)$ by $$ \Sch_l^{\vec{\sigma}}(\Phi) = \extNorm{ 
orm[\vec{x}^{\vec{\sigma}}]_{\F} \cdot \Phi }_l. $$ Here we have written:  egin{itemize} \item $\Norm_l$ is the $\intL^l$-norm on $\F^d$. \item For $\vec{x}=(x_i)_{1 \leq i \leq d} \in \F^d, \vec{\sigma}=(\sigma_i)_{1 \leq i \leq d} \in \ag{R}_{\geq 0}^d$, $
orm[\vec{x}^{\vec{\sigma}}]_{\F}=\Pi_{i=1}^d 
orm[x_i]_{\F}^{\sigma_i}$. \end{itemize} We shall also write $
orm[\vec{\sigma}] = \sum_i \sigma_i$.

nodes.name: Definition 5.20 (the spaces $\fsB_c(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ and $\fsB_c^0(\ag{Z};\varpi)$)
nodes.statement: For any $c \in \ag{R}$, we define $\fsB_c(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ to be the space of functions $f: \varpi^{\ag{Z}} \to \ag{C}$ satisfying \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] $\lim_{n \to -\infty} f(\varpi^n) q^{-n\sigma} = 0$ for any $\sigma > 0$. \item[(2)] $\lim_{n \to +\infty} f(\varpi^n) q^{-n \sigma} = 0$ for any $\sigma > c$. \end{itemize} The subspace $\fsB_c^0(\ag{Z};\varpi) \subset \fsB_c(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ is defined by replacing (1) with \begin{itemize} \item[(1')] $f(\varpi^n)=0$ for $n \ll -1$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Definition 5.21 (the space $\fsH_c(\ag{C};q)$)
nodes.statement: For any $c \in \ag{R}$ we define $\fsH_c(\ag{C};q)$ to be the space of meromorphic functions $M: \ag{C} \to \ag{C}$ satisfying \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] $M(s+i\frac{2\pi}{\log q}) = M(s)$ for all $s \in \ag{C}$. \item[(2)] $M(s)$ is holomorphic for $\Re s > c$. \end{itemize}

Principal congruence subgroup $\Gamma(N)$, $\Gamma_0(N)$, $\Gamma_0^-(N)$ and $n_r^{\pm}(\vec{\alpha})$
nodes.statement: Let $r,N \in \ag{N}, r,N \geq 2$. It is well-known that there is an exact sequence $$ 1 \to \Gamma(N) \to \SL_r(\ag{Z}) \to \SL_r(\ag{Z}/N\ag{Z}) \to 1, $$ where $\Gamma(N)$ is called the principal congruence subgroup of $\SL_r(\ag{Z})$ modulo $N$. The pre-image of the upper resp. lower triangular subgroup of $\SL_r(\ag{Z}/N\ag{Z})$ in $\SL_r(\ag{Z})$ is denoted by $\Gamma_0(N)$ resp. $\Gamma_0^-(N)$, which includes $\Gamma(N)$ as a normal subgroup. For $\vec{\alpha} \in \ag{Z}^{r-1}$ realized as a column vector, we define matrices, with $I_k$ denoting the identity matrix of rank $k$ $$ n_r^+(\vec{\alpha}) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \vec{\alpha}^T \\ \vec{0} & I_{r-1} \end{pmatrix}, n_r^-(\vec{\alpha}) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \vec{0}^T \\ \vec{\alpha} & I_{r-1} \end{pmatrix}. $$
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma_0(N)$ resp. $\Gamma_0^-(N)$ is the preimage in $\SL_r(\ag{Z})$ of the upper resp. lower triangular subgroup mod $N$; $n_r^{\pm}$ are the elementary unipotents.

nodes.name: Canonical embedding $\sigma: \F \to \ag{R}^r$ and the lattice $\sigma(\idlJ)$
nodes.statement: Let $[\F:\ag{Q}]=r=r_1+2r_2$ where $r_1$ resp. $2r_2$ is the number of embeddings of $\F$ into real resp. complex numbers. Recall that we have a canonical map by choosing one complex embedding $\sigma_{r_1+j}, 1 \leq j \leq r_2$ in a pair conjugate to each other by complex conjugation $$ \sigma: \F \to \ag{R}^{r_1} \times \ag{C}^{r_2} \simeq \ag{R}^r, $$ $$ \sigma(x) = (\sigma_1(x), \cdots, \sigma_{r_1+r_2}(x)) = (\sigma_1(x), \cdots, \sigma_{r_1}(x), \Re \sigma_{r_1+1}(x), \Im \sigma_{r_1+1}(x), \cdots, \Re \sigma_{r_1+r_2}(x), \Im \sigma_{r_1+r_2}(x)). $$ For every fractional ideal $\idlJ$, $\sigma(\idlJ)$ is then a $\ag{Z}$-lattice of $\ag{R}^r$.
nodes.statement_short: Realize a number field of degree $r=r_1+2r_2$ inside $\ag{R}^r$ by choosing one embedding from each complex pair, so that fractional ideals become lattices.

nodes.name: The comparison function $f_c$ on $\ag{R}^{r_1} \times \ag{C}^{r_2}$
nodes.statement: For $c \gg 1$, we define a functions $f_c$ on $\ag{R}^{r_1} \times \ag{C}^{r_2}$ by $$ f_c(\vec{x}) = \prod_{i=1}^{r_1} \min(1, \norm[x_i]^{-c}) \prod_{j=1}^{r_2} \min(1, \norm[x_{r_1+j}]^{-2c}), \vec{x}=(x_i)_{1\leq i \leq r_1+r_2}. $$

nodes.name: Valuation exponents $v(\idlJ)$ of an integral ideal
nodes.statement: We shall write, denoting by $\vp_v$ the prime ideal corresponding to $v<\infty$, $v(\idlJ) \in \ag{N}$ such that $$ \idlJ = \prod_{v<\infty} \vp_v^{v(\idlJ)}. $$

nodes.name: Theorem 2.11 (Adelic version of regularization due to Zagier)
nodes.statement: (Adelic version of regularization due to Zagier \cite{Za82}) \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] Let $\varphi: \GL_2(\F)\gp{Z}(\ag{A}) \backslash \GL_2(\ag{A}) \to \ag{C}$ be a slowly increasing function. For $s \in \ag{C}, \Re s \gg 1$ and any $T \gg 1$ we have $$ \int_{[\PGL_2]} \varphi(g) \Lambda^T \Eis(s,f_0)(g) dg = \int_0^T a(t,\varphi)t^{s-\frac{1}{2}} \frac{dt}{t} - \int_T^{\infty} a(t,\varphi) t^{-s-\frac{1}{2}} \frac{dt}{t} \cdot \lambda_{\F}(s-1/2). $$ \item[(2)] If $\varphi$ is, in addition, regularizable, then we have for $T \gg 1$ \begin{align*} &\quad R^*(s,\varphi) + \Lambda_{\F}(1+2s) h_T(s) + \Lambda_{\F}(1-2s) h_T(-s) \\ &= \int_{[\PGL_2]} \varphi(g) \Lambda^T \Eis^*(s,f_0)(g) dg + \\ &\quad \Lambda_{\F}(1+2s) \int_T^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t)) t^{s-\frac{1}{2}} \frac{dt}{t} + \Lambda_{\F}(1-2s) \int_T^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t)) t^{-s-\frac{1}{2}} \frac{dt}{t}. \end{align*} In particular, $R(s,\varphi)$ has a meromorphic continuation to $s \in \ag{C}$ with possible poles at $s=\pm 1/2, \pm \alpha_i, (\rho-1)/2$ for $\rho$ running over the non-trivial zeros of $\zeta_{\F}$, and satisfies the functional equation $$ R^*(s,\varphi) = R^*(-s,\varphi). $$ \item[(3)] Under the condition of (2), if $\Re \alpha_i < 0$ for all $1 \leq i \leq l$, then we have $$ R(s,\varphi) = \int_{[\PGL_2]} \varphi(g) \Eis(s,f_0)(g) dg, \quad \max_{1 \leq i \leq l} \alpha_i < \Re s < -\max_{1 \leq i \leq l} \alpha_i. $$ \item[(4)] Under the condition of (2), if $\varphi$ is integrable on $ [\PGL_2] := \GL_2(\F)\gp{Z}(\ag{A}) \backslash \GL_2(\ag{A}) $, then we have $\Re \alpha_i < 1/2$ for all $1 \leq i \leq l$, and $$ \int_{[\PGL_2]} \varphi(g) dg = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \left( \Res_{s=\frac{1}{2}} R(s,\varphi) + c_i \delta_{\substack{\alpha_i=-\frac{1}{2} \\ n_i=0}} \right), \quad \Vol([\PGL_2]) = \lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0). $$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Rankin-Selberg unfolding against a truncated Eisenstein series gives the meromorphic continuation and functional equation $R^*(s,\varphi)=R^*(-s,\varphi)$, and expresses $\int_{[\PGL_2]}\varphi$ as a residue of $R(s,\varphi)$ at $s=1/2$.
assumptions: Let $\varphi: \GL_2(\F)\gp{Z}(\ag{A}) \backslash \GL_2(\ag{A}) \to \ag{C}$ be a slowly increasing function.
conclusions: $R(s,\varphi)$ has a meromorphic continuation to $s \in \ag{C}$ with possible poles at $s=\pm 1/2, \pm \alpha_i, (\rho-1)/2$ for $\rho$ running over the non-trivial zeros of $\zeta_{\F}$

nodes.name: Theorem 3.4 (regularized integral of a product of two unitary Eisenstein series)
nodes.statement: If $\pi(\xi_1,\xi_2)$ is spherical, we also write The regularized integral of the product of two unitary Eisenstein series is computed as: \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] If $\pi_1 = \pi(\xi_1,\xi_2), \pi_2 = \pi(\xi_1^{-1}, \xi_2^{-1})$ resp. $\pi_2 = \pi(\xi_2^{-1}, \xi_1^{-1})$ and $\xi_1 \neq \xi_2$, then $$ \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \eis(0,f_1) \eis(0,f_2) = \frac{2\lambda_{\F}^{(0)}(0)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1f_2) - \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(\Intw_0^{(1)}f_1 \cdot \Intw_0 f_2), \quad \text{resp.} $$ $$ \frac{\lambda_{\F}^{(0)}(0)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} (\ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1 \Intw_0 f_2) + \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_2 \Intw_0 f_1)) - \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(\Intw_0^{(1)}f_1 \cdot f_2). $$ \item[(2)] If $\pi_1 = \pi(\xi,\xi), \pi_2 = \pi(\xi^{-1},\xi^{-1})$, then \begin{align*} &\quad \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \eis^{(1)}(0,f_1) \eis^{(1)}(0,f_2) = \frac{4\lambda_{\F}^{(2)}(0)}{\lambda_{\F}^{-1}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1f_2) + \frac{4\lambda_{\F}^{(2)}(0)}{\lambda_{\F}^{-1}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1 \cdot \Intw_0^{(1)} f_2) \\ &\quad + \frac{\lambda_{\F}^{(0)}(0)}{\lambda_{\F}^{-1}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(\Intw_0^{(1)}f_1 \cdot \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2) - \frac{1}{3} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(\Intw_0^{(3)}f_1 \cdot f_2) - \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(\Intw_0^{(2)}f_1 \cdot \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2). \end{align*} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit formulas for $\int^{\reg}\eis(0,f_1)\eis(0,f_2)$ and for the product of first derivatives, in terms of $\lambda_{\F}$-coefficients and $\ProjP_{\gp{K}}$ of intertwined products.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.3 (unique ergodicity of the one parameter subgroup $U_{\vec{\theta}}$)
nodes.statement: For any $f \in \Cont(\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}})$, we have $$ \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T f([\vec{x}] + [t.\vec{\theta}]) dt = \int_{\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}}} f dm_{\theta} $$ for all $[\vec{x}] \in \ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}}$. Here $dm_{\theta}$ is the normalized Haar measure on $\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Time averages of a continuous function along the line flow on $\ag{T}_{\vec{\theta}}$ converge to the Haar average.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.1 (vanishing of regularized products in the regular case)
nodes.statement: Let $\xi_j,\xi_j'$ be (unitary) Hecke characters with $\xi_1\xi_1' \xi_2 \xi_2' = 1$ and write $\pi_j = \pi(\xi_j,\xi_j')$, $j=1,2$. For $f_j \in \pi_j$, we shall write $\eis^{\sharp}$ for $\eis$ or $\eis^{\reg}$, whichever is regular at $s=1/2$. If $\pi_1 \not \simeq \widetilde{\pi_2}$, then for any $n_1, n_2 \in \ag{N}$, we have $$ \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \eis^{(n_1)}(0,f_1) \eis^{(n_2)}(0,f_2) = 0, \quad \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \eis^{\sharp,(n_1)}(1/2,f_1) \eis^{\sharp,(n_2)}(1/2,f_2) = 0. $$
nodes.statement_short: If $\pi_1 \not\simeq \widetilde{\pi_2}$, all regularized integrals of products of derivatives of the two Eisenstein series vanish.

nodes.name: Lemma 3.3 (vanishing variant for the unitary series)
nodes.statement: Let $f_1,f_2 \in \Res_{\gp{K}}^{\GL_2(\ag{A})} \pi(1,1)$. For $0 \neq s \in \ag{C}$ small, we have $$ \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \eis(s,f_1) \eis^{(1)}(0,f_2) = 0. $$

nodes.name: Lemma 3.6 (regularized integral of one regularizing Eisenstein series and vanishing of singular products)
nodes.statement: Let $f, f_1, f_2 \in \Res_{\gp{K}}^{\GL_2(\ag{A})} \pi(1,1)$. For $0 \neq s \in \ag{C}$ small, we have for any $n, n_1, n_2 \in \ag{N}$ $$ \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \eis^{\reg, (n)}(\frac{1}{2}+s, f) = -\frac{\lambda_{\F}^{(n)}(s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f); $$ $$ \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \eis^{\reg, (n_1)}(\frac{1}{2}+s, f_1) \eis^{\reg, (n_2)}(\frac{1}{2}, f_2) = 0. $$
nodes.statement_short: The regularized integral of $\eis^{\reg,(n)}(1/2+s,f)$ is $-\lambda_{\F}^{(n)}(s)/\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)$ times $\ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f)$, and the mixed product with $\eis^{\reg,(n_2)}(1/2,f_2)$ vanishes.

nodes.statement: Any coset of $\Gamma_0(N) \backslash \SL_r(\ag{Z})$ resp. $\Gamma_0^-(N) \backslash \SL_r(\ag{Z})$ has a representative of the form $N_- N_+$ resp. $N_+N_-$, where $N_-$ resp. $N_+$ is lower resp. upper unipotent with off-diagonal entries lying in $[-\frac{N}{2}, \frac{N}{2}] \cap \ag{Z}$.

nodes.name: Proposition 2.20 (stability of $\Aut^{\freg}$ under right translation)
nodes.statement: $\Aut^{\freg}(\GL_2,\omega)$ is stable under the right translation by $\GL_2(\ag{A})$. Moreover, for any $\varphi \in \Aut^{\freg}(\GL_2,\omega)$ and any $g \in \GL_2(\ag{A})$, their sets of exponents are the same: $$ \Ex(g.\varphi) = \Ex(\varphi). $$
conclusions: $\Aut^{\freg}(\GL_2,\omega)$ is stable under the right translation by $\GL_2(\ag{A})$

nodes.name: Proposition 2.21 (stability of $\Reis^+(\GL_2,\omega)$ under right translation)
nodes.statement: The vector space $\Reis^+(\GL_2, \omega)$ is stable under the right translation by $\GL_2(\ag{A})$.
conclusions: The vector space $\Reis^+(\GL_2, \omega)$ is stable under the right translation by $\GL_2(\ag{A})$.

nodes.name: Proposition 2.24 (existence and uniqueness of the residual part $\Reis(\varphi)$)
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi \in \Aut^{\freg}(\GL_2,\omega)$. \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] We can always find (not unique) $\Reis(\varphi) \in \Reis(\GL_2,\omega)$ such that $\varphi - \Reis(\varphi) \in \intL^1(\GL_2, \omega)$. \item[(2)] If for any $\chi \in \Ex(\varphi)$, we have $\Re \chi \neq 1/2$, then there is a unique function $\Reis(\varphi) \in \Reis(\GL_2,\omega)$ such that $\varphi - \Reis(\varphi) \in \intL^2(\GL_2, \omega)$. Moreover, for any $X$ in the universal enveloping algebra of $\GL_2(\ag{A}_{\infty})$, we have $X.\varphi - X.\Reis(\varphi) \in \intL^2(\GL_2, \omega)$, i.e., $\Reis(X.\varphi) = X.\Reis(\varphi)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Every finitely regularizable $\varphi$ admits a residual $\Reis(\varphi)$ making the difference $\intL^1$; away from $\Re \chi = 1/2$ it is unique, $\intL^2$ and commutes with the universal enveloping algebra.
conclusions: We can always find (not unique) $\Reis(\varphi) \in \Reis(\GL_2,\omega)$ such that $\varphi - \Reis(\varphi) \in \intL^1(\GL_2, \omega)$

nodes.name: Proposition 2.26 ($\gp{K}$-invariance of the regularized integral and vanishing on the residual space)
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item[(1)] For any $\Reis \in \Reis(\GL_2,1)$, we have $$ \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \Reis(g) dg = 0. $$ If moreover $\Reis \in \Reis^+(\GL_2,1)$, then for any $g_0 \in \GL_2(\ag{A})$, we have $$ \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} g_0.\Reis(g) dg = 0. $$ \item[(2)] Let $\varphi \in \Aut^{\freg}(\GL_2,1)$. For any $\Reis \in \Reis(\GL_2,1)$ such that $\varphi - \Reis \in \intL^1([\PGL_2])$ we have $$ \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \varphi(g) dg = \int_{[\PGL_2]} (\varphi-\Reis)(g) dg. $$ In particular, $\int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg}$ is always $\gp{K}$-invariant. It is $\GL_2(\ag{A})$-invariant on the subspace of $\varphi \in \Aut^{\freg}(\GL_2,1)$ such that $\Ex(\varphi)$ does not contain $\norm_{\ag{A}}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: The regularized integral kills the residual space, computes $\int(\varphi-\Reis)$, is always $\gp{K}$-invariant, and is $\GL_2(\ag{A})$-invariant exactly off the singular exponent $\norm_{\ag{A}}$.

nodes.name: Proposition 4.1 (meromorphic continuation of the variant $R(s,\varphi;f)$)
nodes.statement: For $\Re s \gg 1$ sufficiently large, $$ R(s,\varphi; f) := \int_{\F^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{\times}} \int_{\gp{K}} (\varphi_{\gp{N}} - \varphi_{\gp{N}}^*)(a(y)\kappa) f(\kappa) \xi_1(y) \norm[y]_{\ag{A}}^{s-\frac{1}{2}} d\kappa d^{\times}y $$ is absolutely convergent. It has a meromorphic continuation to $s \in \ag{C}$. If in addition $$ \Theta := \max_j \{ \Re \alpha_j \} < 0, $$ then we have, with the right hand side absolutely converging $$ R(s,\varphi; f) = \int_{[\PGL_2]} \varphi \cdot \eis(s,f), \quad \Theta < \Re s < -\Theta. $$ In the above region, the possible poles of $R(s, \varphi; f)$ are \begin{itemize} \item $1/2 + i\mu(\xi_1\xi_2^{-1})$ if $\xi_1 \xi_2^{-1}$ is trivial on $\ag{A}^{(1)}$; \item $(\rho - 1)/2$ where $\rho$ runs over the non-trivial zeros of $L(s,\xi_1\xi_2^{-1})$. \end{itemize} In particular $R(s,\varphi; f)$ is holomorphic for $0 \leq \Re s < \min(-\Theta,1/2)$.
nodes.statement_short: The twisted Rankin-Selberg integral $R(s,\varphi;f)$ converges for $\Re s \gg 1$, continues meromorphically, equals $\int \varphi \cdot \eis(s,f)$ in a strip, and is holomorphic for $0 \le \Re s < \min(-\Theta,1/2)$.

In particular $R(s,\varphi; f)$ is holomorphic for $0 \leq \Re s < \min(-\Theta,1/2)$.

nodes.statement: The topology on $\fsB_c(\ag{R}_+)$ defined by $B_l^{k,\sigma}$ does not depend on $l$. More precisely, for any $f \in \fsB_c(\ag{R}_+)$ we have for $1 \leq l < \infty$ and $\epsilon > 0$ small with $\sigma - \epsilon > c$ $$ B_l^{k,\sigma}(f) \ll_{\epsilon, l} B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma + \epsilon}(f) + B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma - \epsilon}(f); $$ $$ B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(f) \ll_{\epsilon, l, \sigma + k} B_l^{k,\sigma }(f) + B_l^{k+1,\sigma}(f). $$

nodes.name: Proposition 5.12 ($l$-independence of the topology on $\fsH_c(\ag{C})$)
nodes.statement: The topology on $\fsH_c(\ag{C})$ defined by $H_l^{k,\sigma}$ does not depend on $l$. More precisely, for any $M \in \fsH_c(\ag{C})$ we have for $1 \leq l < \infty$ and $\epsilon > 0$ small with $\sigma - \epsilon > c$ $$ H_l^{k,\sigma}(M) \ll_{k, l} H_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(M) + H_{\infty}^{k+2,\sigma}(M); $$ $$ H_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(M) \ll_{\epsilon, l, \sigma + k} H_l^{k,\sigma+\epsilon}(M) + H_l^{k+1,\sigma+\epsilon}(M) + H_l^{k,\sigma-\epsilon}(M) + H_l^{k+1,\sigma-\epsilon}(M). $$

nodes.name: Proposition 5.17 (relations between $D(\Phi)$, $\delta(\Phi)$, $m(\Phi)$ under Fourier transform)
nodes.statement: The three indices satisfy the following relations. \begin{itemize} \item[(0)] $m(\Phi) \leq \delta(\Phi)-D(\Phi)$. \item[(1)] For any $\kappa \in \GL_d(\vo)$, we have $D(\rpR(\kappa).\Phi)=D(\Phi)$, $\delta(\rpR(\kappa).\Phi)=\delta(\Phi)$ and $m(\rpR(\kappa).\Phi)=m(\Phi)$. \item[(2)] Let $\Four{\cdot}$ denote the Fourier transform $$ \Four{\Phi}(\vec{x}) = \int_{\F^d} \Phi(\vec{y}) \psi(-\vec{y}.\vec{x}) d\vec{y}. $$ Then we have $$ D(\Phi)+\delta(\Four{\Phi}) = \delta(\Phi) + D(\Four{\Phi}) = -\cond(\psi). $$ \item[(3)] More generally, let $I = \{ i_1, \cdots, i_j \} \subset \{ 1, \dots, d \}$. We define the partial Fourier transform $\Four[I]{\cdot} = \Four[i_1]{\Four[i_2]{ \cdots \Four[i_j]{\cdot}}}$. Then we have $$ \delta(\Four[I]{\Phi})) \leq \max(\delta(\Phi), -\cond(\psi)-D(\Phi)); $$ $$ D(\Four[I]{\Phi}) \geq \min(D(\Phi), -\cond(\psi)-\delta(\Phi)). $$ \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: The three indices are invariant under $\GL_d(\vo)$, satisfy $m \le \delta - D$, and are exchanged by the Fourier transform via $D(\Phi)+\delta(\Four{\Phi}) = \delta(\Phi)+D(\Four{\Phi}) = -\cond(\psi)$.

nodes.name: Proposition 5.19 (comparison of $\intL^l$ and sup norms on $\Sch(\F^d)$)

nodes.name: Proposition 5.24 ($l$-independence of the topology on $\fsB_c(\ag{Z};\varpi)$)

More precisely, for any $f \in \fsB_c(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ we have for $1 \leq l < \infty$ and $\epsilon > 0$ small with $\sigma - \epsilon > c$ $$ B_l^{\sigma}(f) \ll_{\epsilon,l} B_{\infty}^{\sigma-\epsilon}(f) + B_{\infty}^{\sigma+\epsilon}(f); $$ $$ B_{\infty}^{\sigma}(f) \leq B_l^{\sigma}(f). $$
assumptions: for any $f \in \fsB_c(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ we have for $1 \leq l < \infty$ and $\epsilon > 0$ small with $\sigma - \epsilon > c$

nodes.name: Proposition 5.25 ($l$-independence of the topology on $\fsH_c(\ag{C};q)$)
nodes.statement: The topology on $\fsH_c(\ag{C};q)$ defined by $H_l^*$ does not depend on $l$. More precisely, for any $M \in \fsH_c(\ag{C};q)$ we have for $1 \leq l < \infty$ and $\epsilon > 0$ small with $\sigma - \epsilon > c$ $$ H_l^{\sigma}(M) \leq H_{\infty}^{\sigma}(M); $$ $$ H_{\infty}^{\sigma}(M) \ll_{\epsilon} H_l^{\sigma-\epsilon}(M) + H_l^{\sigma+\epsilon}(M). $$
assumptions: for any $M \in \fsH_c(\ag{C};q)$ we have for $1 \leq l < \infty$ and $\epsilon > 0$ small with $\sigma - \epsilon > c$

nodes.name: Proposition 5.27 (finiteness of nonzero $\F^1$-components and their bound)
nodes.statement: For any $f \in \Sch(\F)$, $f_{\xi} \neq 0$ only for $\xi$ satisfying $\cond(\xi) \leq m(f)$, hence for only finitely many $\xi$. We have $f_{\xi} \in B_0^0(\ag{Z};\varpi)$ and $$ B_{\infty}^{\sigma}(f_{\xi}) \leq \Sch_{\infty}^{\sigma}(f), \forall \sigma > 0. $$

conclusions: $f_{\xi} \neq 0$ only for $\xi$ satisfying $\cond(\xi) \leq m(f)$, hence for only finitely many $\xi$

nodes.name: Proposition 5.30 (rapid decay of the non constant part of the smooth Eisenstein series)
nodes.statement: For any $\Phi \in \Sch(\ag{A}^2)$, $m \in \ag{N}$ and any $\sigma > \norm[\Re s]$, we have $$ \extnorm{\frac{\partial^m}{\partial s^m} \left( \Eis(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\Phi)(g) - \eisCst(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\Phi)(g) \right)} \leq \sum_{\alpha \in \F^{\times}} \extnorm{\frac{\partial^m}{\partial s^m} W_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};a(\alpha)g)} \ll_{\sigma,\Phi} \Ht(g)^{-\frac{1}{2}-\sigma}, $$ which is of rapid decay with respect to $\Ht(g)$.

nodes.statement: The possible poles of the collection of meromorphic functions $\{ \mu(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};\vec{n}) : \vec{n} \}$ are \begin{itemize} \item The pole of $\Lambda(1-2s,\omega\xi^{-2})$ at $s=(1+i\mu(\omega\xi^{-2}))/2$ with order at most $1$, when $\omega\xi^{-2}$ is trivial on $\ag{A}^{(1)}$ and $\vec{n}=\vec{0}$. We call this pole the \emph{spherical pole}. \item The (both trivial and non-trivial) zeros of $L(1+2s,\omega^{-1}\xi^2)$ with order at most that of the zero. \end{itemize}

nodes.statement: In the case $\omega=1$, a finitely regularizable is smooth and regularizable in the sense of Definition \ref{RegFuncDef}. But a smooth regularizable function doesn't need to be finitely regularizable.

nodes.name: Remark 2.16 (Hecke operators almost annihilate $\eis^{\reg}(1/2,e_0)$)
nodes.statement: Let $e_0 \in \Res_{\gp{K}}^{\GL_2(\ag{A})} \pi(1,1)$ be the spherical function taking value $1$ on $\gp{K}$. Let $T(\vp)$ denote the order $1$ Hecke operator at a finite place $\vp$ with cardinality of the residue field $q$. For $s \neq 0$, we have $$ T(\vp). \eis(\frac{1}{2}+s, e_0) = \lambda_{\vp}(s) \eis(\frac{1}{2}+s, e_0), \quad \lambda_{\vp}(s) = \frac{q^{1/2+s} + q^{-(1/2+s)}}{q^{1/2}+q^{-1/2}}; $$ $$ \text{or} \quad T(\vp). \eis^{\reg}(\frac{1}{2}+s, e_0) = \lambda_{\vp}(s) \eis^{\reg}(\frac{1}{2}+s, e_0) + (\lambda_{\vp}(s)-1) \cdot \lambda_{\F}(s). $$ The pole of $\lambda_{\F}(s)$, defined in (\ref{lambdaFDef}), at $s=0$ is compensated by the zero of $\lambda_{\vp}(s)-1$, hence we get $$ T(\vp). \eis^{\reg}(\frac{1}{2}, e_0) = \eis^{\reg}(\frac{1}{2}, e_0) + \lambda_{\vp}^{(1)}(0) \cdot \lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0). $$ In particular, $(T(\vp)-1)^2$ annihilates $\eis^{\reg}(1/2,e_0)$.
nodes.statement_short: $T(\vp)$ acts on $\eis^{\reg}(1/2,e_0)$ by $1$ plus a constant, so $(T(\vp)-1)^2$ annihilates it.

nodes.name: Remark 2.17 (Violation of Covariance)
nodes.statement: Unlike the usual Eisenstein series, the map $$ \pi^{\infty}(\xi \norm^{(1-i\mu)/2}, \omega\xi^{-1} \norm^{-(1-i\mu)/2}) \to \Cont^{\infty}(\GL_2, \omega), \quad f_{(1-i\mu)/2} \mapsto \eis^{\reg}((1-i\mu)/2, f) $$ is \emph{NOT} $\GL_2(\ag{A})$-covariant. But it's still $\gp{K}$-covariant.
nodes.statement_short: The map $f \mapsto \eis^{\reg}$ is only $\gp{K}$-covariant, not $\GL_2(\ag{A})$-covariant.

nodes.name: Remark 2.18 (examples of finitely regularizable functions)
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{GlobRDEisWhi}, \ref{GlobRDEisCst} and the definition of cusp forms, $\Aut^{\freg}(\GL_2,\omega)$ contains: \begin{itemize} \item $\chi(\det g)$ for quasi-characters $\chi$ such that $\chi^2=\omega$; \item smooth cusp forms, i.e., $\Aut_{\cusp}^{\infty}(\GL_2,\omega)$; \item $\frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n}\Eis(s,f)$ for some $n \in \ag{N}$ and smooth $f \in \Ind_{\gp{B}(\ag{A})}^{\GL_2(\ag{A})}(\xi, \omega\xi^{-1})$ with $\Re s \geq 0$ and $s \neq -i\mu/2, 1/2-i\mu/2$ for $\mu=\mu(\omega^{-1}\xi^2)$ if $\omega\xi^{-2}$ is trivial on $\ag{A}^{(1)}$; \item $\frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} \mid_{s=-i\frac{\mu}{2}} (s+i\frac{\mu}{2})\Eis^*(s,f)$ for some $n \in \ag{N}$ and smooth $f$, $\mu$ the same as above; \item $\frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n}\Eis^{\reg}(\frac{1-i\mu}{2},f)$ for some $n \in \ag{N}$ and $f,\mu$ the same as above; \item $\varphi=\Pi_{j=1}^l \varphi_j$ where $\varphi_j \in \Aut^{\freg}(\GL_2,\omega_j)$ with $\omega = \Pi_j \omega_j$. \end{itemize} In the last case, we have $ \varphi_{\gp{N}}^* = \Pi_j \varphi_{j,\gp{N}}^* $. Note that we have excluded $\Eis(s,f)$ for $\Re s < 0$. But they are actually present since they are related to the case $\Re s > 0$ by functional equation.
nodes.statement_short: $\Aut^{\freg}(\GL_2,\omega)$ contains quasi-characters of the determinant, smooth cusp forms, $s$-derivatives of (regularizing) Eisenstein series, and products of such.

nodes.name: Remark 5.1 (abbreviated notation $\Eis(s,f)$)
nodes.statement: We will sometimes omit $\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}$ and write $\Eis(s,f)$ when it is clear from the context.

nodes.name: Remark 5.6 (semi-norms on $\Sch(\ag{C})$ via $\ag{C} \simeq \ag{R}^2$)
nodes.statement: Since $\ag{C} \simeq \ag{R}^2$, we put the semi-norms for $\Sch(\ag{R}^2)$ on $\Sch(\ag{C})$.

nodes.name: Remark 5.7 (convention on unspecified Schwartz norms)
nodes.statement: If we do not specify the parameters of a Schwartz norm $\Sch^*$, we mean the max of a finite collection of Schwartz norms. This applies to Lemma \ref{SchNormEquivA}, \ref{IntBdA} and Proposition \ref{LocWhiBdA}.

nodes.name: Remark 5.34 (the coefficient $f_0$ at the spherical pole)
nodes.statement: If $s_0$ is the spherical pole, then $n=1$ and for $m=0$ we have $f_k=0$ unless $k=0$. Then $$ f_0(\kappa) = \lim_{s \to s_0} \frac{(s-s_0)\Lambda_{\F}(2(s_0-s)}{\Lambda_{\F}(2-2(s_0-s)))} \int_{\gp{K}} f(\kappa) d\kappa = - \frac{\Lambda_{\F}^*(0)}{\Lambda_{\F}(2)} \int_{\gp{K}} f(\kappa) d\kappa. $$
nodes.statement_short: At the spherical pole the only surviving coefficient is $f_0(\kappa) = -\frac{\Lambda_{\F}^*(0)}{\Lambda_{\F}(2)} \int_{\gp{K}} f$.

nodes.name: Vanishing limit of a sum of unitary characters
nodes.statement: \lim_{T \to \infty} \sum c_j T^{i\tau_j} = 0
nodes.statement_short: The limit relation that the two cases of the proof both reduce to.

nodes.name: Definition and Taylor expansion of $\lambda_{\F}(s)$
nodes.statement: \lambda_{\F}(s) := \frac{\Lambda_{\F}(-2s)}{\Lambda_{\F}(2+2s)} = \frac{\lambda_{\F}^{-1}(0)}{s} + \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{s^n}{n!} \lambda_{\F}^{(n)}(0).
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda_{\F}(s) = \Lambda_{\F}(-2s)/\Lambda_{\F}(2+2s)$ has a simple pole at $s=0$ with Laurent coefficients $\lambda_{\F}^{(n)}(0)$.

nodes.name: Explicit choice of the residual part $\Reis(\varphi)$
nodes.statement: \Reis(\varphi) = \sum_{\substack{\Re \alpha_j > 0 \\ \alpha_j \neq \frac{1}{2}+i\mu_j}} \frac{\partial^{n_j}}{\partial s^{n_j}}\Eis(\alpha_j,\omega,\omega^{-1}\chi_j;f_j) + \sum_{\substack{\Re \alpha_j > 0 \\ \alpha_j = \frac{1}{2}+i\mu_j}} \frac{\partial^{n_j}}{\partial s^{n_j}}\Eis^{\reg}(\alpha_j,\omega,\omega^{-1}\chi_j;f_j).
nodes.statement_short: Build $\Reis(\varphi)$ from Eisenstein series at the exponents with $\Re \alpha_j > 0$, using regularizing ones at the singular exponent.

nodes.name: The deformation principle
nodes.statement: \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \varphi = \int_{[\PGL_2]} \varphi - \Reis = \lim_{s \to 0} \int_{[\PGL_2]} \varphi_s - \Reis_s = \lim_{s \to 0} \left( \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \varphi_s - \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \Reis_s \right).
nodes.statement_short: Compute a regularized integral as the $s \to 0$ limit of regularized integrals of deformed families minus their residual parts.

nodes.name: Relation between $f_{\Phi}$ and the flat section $f_s$
nodes.statement: f_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};g) = \Dis(\F)^{\frac{1}{2}}\Lambda^S(1+2s,\omega^{-1}\xi^2) \prod_{\substack{v \in S \\ v \mid \infty}} K_{v,a_v}(s,\omega_v^{-1}\xi_v^2) \cdot f_s(g).
nodes.statement_short: $f_{\Phi}$ equals an explicit product of partial $\Lambda$-factors and archimedean $K$-factors times the flat section $f_s$.

nodes.name: Schwartz-function integral representation $W_{\Phi}$ of the Whittaker function
nodes.statement: W_{\Phi}(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}; g) = \xi(\det g)\norm[\det g]_{\ag{A}}^{\frac{1}{2}+s} \int_{\ag{A}^{\times}} \Four[2]{\rpR(g).\Phi}(t,\frac{1}{t}) \omega^{-1}\xi^2(t)\norm[t]_{\ag{A}}^{2s} d^{\times}t,
nodes.statement_short: $W_{\Phi}$ is a zeta-type integral of the partial Fourier transform of $\rpR(g).\Phi$ along the anti-diagonal.

nodes.name: Setting for the complements: Hecke characters with $\xi_1 \xi_2 \omega = 1$
nodes.statement: Let $\xi_1,\xi_2, \omega$ be Hecke characters with $\xi_1 \xi_2 \omega =1$. Let $f \in \pi(\xi_1,\xi_2)$ and $\varphi \in \Cont^{\infty}(\GL_2, \omega)$, i.e., a smooth function on $\GL_2(\F) \backslash \GL_2(\ag{A})$ with central character $\omega$. Suppose $\varphi$ is \emph{finitely regularizable} defined in Definition \ref{FinRegFuncDef}.
nodes.statement_short: Fix Hecke characters with $\xi_1\xi_2\omega=1$, a section $f \in \pi(\xi_1,\xi_2)$, and a finitely regularizable $\varphi$ of central character $\omega$.

nodes.name: Appendix setting: notations and assumptions of the companion paper
nodes.statement: We take the notations and assumptions in \cite{Wu5}. Namely we fix a section $s_{\F}: \ag{R}_+ \to \F^{\times} \backslash \ag{A}^{\times}$ and assume the Hecke characters $\omega, \xi$ to be trivial on the image of $s_{\F}$. We then have the definition of the Eisenstein series $\Eis(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)$ for $f \in V_{\xi,\omega\xi^{-1}}^{\infty}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the norm section $s_{\F}$ and assume $\omega, \xi$ are trivial on its image, so that $\Eis(s,\xi,\omega\xi^{-1};f)$ is defined.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.4
nodes.statement: Note that $f(e^{2\pi t}) = \sum_{k=1}^n a_k e(t\theta_k), t \in \ag{R}$. If $f$ is not constant, we can find $t_1, t_2 \in \ag{R}$ s.t. $f(e^{2\pi t_1}) \neq f(e^{2\pi t_2})$. By continuity, we then find some neighborhood $U_1$ of $[t_1 \vec{\theta}]$, and $U_2$ of $[t_2 \vec{\theta}]$ such that $$ \sum_{k=1}^n a_k e(x_k) \neq \sum_{k=1}^n a_k e(y_k), \forall \vec{x} \in U_1, \vec{y} \in U_2. $$ But the flow $\gamma(t) = [t\vec{\theta}]$ meets both $U_1$ and $U_2$ infinitely often by the lemma, hence $\lim_{t \to \infty} f(e^{2\pi t})$ can not exist, contradicting the hypothesis.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: if $f$ is non constant, separate two values by neighborhoods which the (uniquely ergodic) line flow visits infinitely often.

nodes.name: Assume $f$ non constant and separate two values
nodes.statement: Note that $f(e^{2\pi t}) = \sum_{k=1}^n a_k e(t\theta_k), t \in \ag{R}$. If $f$ is not constant, we can find $t_1, t_2 \in \ag{R}$ s.t. $f(e^{2\pi t_1}) \neq f(e^{2\pi t_2})$. By continuity, we then find some neighborhood $U_1$ of $[t_1 \vec{\theta}]$, and $U_2$ of $[t_2 \vec{\theta}]$ such that $$ \sum_{k=1}^n a_k e(x_k) \neq \sum_{k=1}^n a_k e(y_k), \forall \vec{x} \in U_1, \vec{y} \in U_2. $$
nodes.statement_short: Pick $t_1,t_2$ with $f(e^{2\pi t_1}) \neq f(e^{2\pi t_2})$ and separate them by neighborhoods $U_1,U_2$.

nodes.name: The flow meets both neighborhoods infinitely often
nodes.statement: But the flow $\gamma(t) = [t\vec{\theta}]$ meets both $U_1$ and $U_2$ infinitely often by the lemma, hence $\lim_{t \to \infty} f(e^{2\pi t})$ can not exist, contradicting the hypothesis.
nodes.statement_short: By the lemma the limit cannot exist, contradicting the hypothesis.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.11
nodes.statement:
Since the proofs of (1) to (3) are quite similar to that in \cite{Za82}, we only mention some essential points of them. Only (4) needs more explanation. 
oindent (1) This is standard Rankin-Selberg unfolding together with $$ \Lambda^T \Eis(s,f_0)(g) = \sum_{\gamma \in \gp{B}(\F)  ackslash \GL_2(\F)} f_{0,s}(\gamma g) 1_{\Ht(\gamma g) \leq T} - \sum_{\gamma \in \gp{B}(\F)  ackslash \GL_2(\F)} \Intw f_{0,s}(\gamma g) 1_{\Ht(\gamma g) > T}. $$ 
oindent (2) It follows from rewriting the two terms at the right hand side of (1). For the first term we have  egin{align*} \int_0^T a(t,\varphi) t^{s- rac{1}{2}}  rac{dt}{t} &= R(s,\varphi) - \int_T^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t)) t^{s- rac{1}{2}}  rac{dt}{t} + \sum_{i=1}^l  rac{c_i}{n_i!} \int_0^T t^{s+\alpha_i} \log^{n_i} t  rac{dt}{t} \ &= R(s,\varphi) - \int_T^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t)) t^{s- rac{1}{2}}  rac{dt}{t} + h_T(s). \end{align*} For the second term we have a similar equality. 
oindent (3) In the case $\Re \alpha_i < 0$ for all $i$, we let $T 	o \infty$, taking into account Proposition ef{GlobRDEisWhi} and $h_T(s) 	o 0$, to get the asserted equation. 
oindent (4) The integrability of $\varphi$ implies $\Re \alpha_i < 1/2$ for all $i$ by Lemma ef{IntExpBd}. We take residue at $s=1/2$ on both sides of the equation obtained in (2) and divide by $\Lambda_{\F}(1+2s)$ to see for $T \gg 1$  egin{align*} &\quad \Res_{s= rac{1}{2}} R(s,\varphi) + \Res_{s= rac{1}{2}} h_T(s) + \lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0) h_T(- rac{1}{2}) \ &= \lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0) \int_{\FundD_T} \varphi(g)dg + \Res_{s= rac{1}{2}} \int_{\FundD-\FundD_T} \varphi(g) \left( \Eis(s,f_0)(g) - \Eis(s,f_0)_N(g) ight) dg \ &\quad + \lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0) \int_T^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t))  rac{dt}{t^2}, \end{align*} where $\FundD$ is the standard fundamental domain for $[\PGL_2]$ and $\FundD_T$ is the set of $g \in \FundD$ such that $\Ht(g) \leq T$. It is easy to see that as $T 	o \infty$ $$ h_T(- rac{1}{2}) 	o 0; \quad \int_T^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t))  rac{dt}{t^2} 	o 0. $$ By Proposition ef{GlobRDEisWhi}, $\Eis(s,f_0)(g) - \Eis(s,f_0)_N(g)$ is of uniformly rapid decay with respect to $\Ht(g), g \in \FundD$ as $s$ remains in a compact neighborhood of $1/2$. Hence $$ \int_{\FundD-\FundD_T} \varphi(g) \left( \Eis(s,f_0)(g) - \Eis(s,f_0)_N(g) ight) dg $$ is holomorphic at $s=1/2$. We compute $\Res_{s= rac{1}{2}} h_T(s)$ by noting that the second summand of $$  rac{d^n}{d s^n} \left(  rac{T^s}{s} ight) =  rac{(-1)^n n!}{s^{n+1}} + \int_0^{\log T} t^n e^{st} dt $$ is holomorphic at $s=0$, and get $$ \Res_{s= rac{1}{2}} h_T(s) = c_i \delta_{\substack{\alpha_i=- rac{1}{2} \ n_i=0}}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Rankin-Selberg unfolding for (1), rewriting of the two truncated tails for (2), letting $T \to \infty$ for (3), and a residue computation at $s=1/2$ for (4).

nodes.name: Announce which parts are treated
nodes.statement: Since the proofs of (1) to (3) are quite similar to that in \cite{Za82}, we only mention some essential points of them. Only (4) needs more explanation.
nodes.statement_short: Only essential points of (1)-(3) are given; (4) is treated in detail.

nodes.name: Part (1): Rankin-Selberg unfolding of the truncated Eisenstein series
nodes.statement: \noindent (1) This is standard Rankin-Selberg unfolding together with $$ \Lambda^T \Eis(s,f_0)(g) = \sum_{\gamma \in \gp{B}(\F) \backslash \GL_2(\F)} f_{0,s}(\gamma g) 1_{\Ht(\gamma g) \leq T} - \sum_{\gamma \in \gp{B}(\F) \backslash \GL_2(\F)} \Intw f_{0,s}(\gamma g) 1_{\Ht(\gamma g) > T}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Unfold using the two-sum expression for $\Lambda^T \Eis(s,f_0)$.

nodes.name: Part (2): rewrite the two truncated integrals via $h_T(s)$
nodes.statement: \noindent (2) It follows from rewriting the two terms at the right hand side of (1). For the first term we have \begin{align*} \int_0^T a(t,\varphi) t^{s-\frac{1}{2}} \frac{dt}{t} &= R(s,\varphi) - \int_T^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t)) t^{s-\frac{1}{2}} \frac{dt}{t} + \sum_{i=1}^l \frac{c_i}{n_i!} \int_0^T t^{s+\alpha_i} \log^{n_i} t \frac{dt}{t} \\ &= R(s,\varphi) - \int_T^{\infty} (a(t,\varphi)-f(t)) t^{s-\frac{1}{2}} \frac{dt}{t} + h_T(s). \end{align*} For the second term we have a similar equality.
nodes.statement_short: Add and subtract $f(t)$ to convert each truncated integral into $R(s,\varphi)$ plus a tail plus $h_T(s)$.

nodes.name: Part (3): let $T \to \infty$ using rapid decay
nodes.statement: \noindent (3) In the case $\Re \alpha_i < 0$ for all $i$, we let $T \to \infty$, taking into account Proposition \ref{GlobRDEisWhi} and $h_T(s) \to 0$, to get the asserted equation.
nodes.statement_short: When all $\Re \alpha_i<0$, Proposition 5.30 and $h_T(s)\to 0$ give the asserted identity.

nodes.name: Part (4): take residues at $s=1/2$ and identify the degenerate term
nodes.statement: \noindent (4) The integrability of $\varphi$ implies $\Re \alpha_i < 1/2$ for all $i$ by Lemma \ref{IntExpBd}. Let $e_{\vec{k}}$ be an orthonormal $\gp{K}$-isotypic basis of $\Res_{\gp{K}}^{\GL_2(\ag{A})} \pi(\xi, \omega\xi^{-1})$. There is an orthonormal $\gp{K}$-isotypic basis $\tilde{e}_{\vec{k}}$ of $\Res_{\gp{K}}^{\GL_2(\ag{A})} \pi(\omega\xi^{-1}, \xi)$ and for any $n \in \ag{N}$ there is $A > 0$ such that (c.f. \cite[\S 3]{Wu5}) $$ \Intw_s e_{\vec{k},s} = \mu_{\vec{k}}(s) \tilde{e}_{\vec{k},-s}, \quad \extnorm{\mu_{\vec{k}}^{(n)}(s)} \ll \lambda_{\vec{k}}^A $$ for some meromorphic function $\mu_{\vec{k}}(s)$, regular in $\Re s > 0, s \neq 1/2$. Here $\lambda_{\vec{k}}$ is the eigenvalue of the Laplacian on $\gp{K}_{\infty}$ for $e_{\vec{k}}$, and the bound is uniform for $s$ lying in any compact subset of the regular region. We also have an expansion $$ g.f_s = \sideset{}{_{\vec{k}}} \sum a_{\vec{k}}(s,g) e_{\vec{k},s}, $$ for some functions $a_{\vec{k}}(s,g)$ holomorphic in $s$ and smooth in $g$, since $$ a_{\vec{k}}(s,g) = \int_{\gp{K}} f_s(\kappa g) \overline{e_{\vec{k}}(\kappa)} d\kappa. $$ Moreover, we have $ a_{\vec{k}}(s,g) \ll_{g,f,N} \lambda_{\vec{k}}^{-N} $ for any $N \in \ag{N}$, uniformly for $s$ lying in any compact neighborhood of $s_0$. It follows that for any $l \in \ag{N}$ $$ a_{\vec{k}}^{(l)}(s,g) := \frac{\partial^l}{\partial s^l} \mid_{s=s_0} a_{\vec{k}}(s,g) \ll_{g,f,N} \lambda_{\vec{k}}^{-N}. $$ We thus get $$ g.f_{s_0}^{(n)} = \sideset{}{_{k=0}^n} \sum \sideset{}{_{\vec{k}}} \sum \binom{n}{k} a_{\vec{k}}^{(n-k)}(s_0,g) e_{\vec{k},s_0}^{(k)}. $$ The inner sum coincides with the value at $s=s_0$ of a flat section $f_{k,s}^{(k)}$ defined by $$ f_k = \binom{n}{k} \sideset{}{_{\vec{k}}} \sum a_{\vec{k}}^{(n-k)}(s_0,g) e_{\vec{k}}, $$ which is smooth. nodes.statement: \item $\Reis(g)=\frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} \Eis^{\reg}(\frac{1}{2}-i\mu(\chi),f)(g)$: We get \begin{align*} a(t,\Reis) &= \zeta_{\F}^*(1) \int_{\gp{K}} f(k)dk \cdot \\ &\quad \left\{ t \log^n t + \frac{\partial^n}{\partial s^n} \mid_{s=\frac{1}{2}-i\mu(\chi)} \left( (t^{\frac{1}{2}-s-i\mu(\chi)}-1) \frac{\Lambda_{\F}(1-2s-2i\mu(\chi))}{\Lambda_{\F}(1+2s+2i\mu(\chi))} \right) \right\} \\ &= \zeta_{\F}^*(1) \int_{\gp{K}} f(k)dk \cdot \\ &\quad \left\{ t \log^n t + \sum_{l=0}^n \binom{n}{l} \frac{(-1)^l}{l+1} \cdot \log^{l+1}t \cdot \frac{d^{n-l}}{d s^{n-l}} \mid_{s=0} \left( \frac{s\Lambda_{\F}(2s)}{\Lambda_{\F}(2-2s)} \right) \right\}, \end{align*} and conclude the same way as in the previous case.
nodes.statement_short: Expanding the difference quotient again yields no constant term in $t$.

nodes.name: Deduce part (2) and the invariance statements
nodes.statement: For (2), the first part is trivial. For the second part, we note that $\varphi-\Reis(\varphi) \in \intL^1$ implies $g_0.\varphi-g_0.\Reis(\varphi) \in \intL^1$ for any $g_0 \in \GL_2(\ag{A})$, and $g_0.\Reis(\varphi)$ has regularized integral $0$ by (1) if either $\Reis \in \Reis^+(\GL_2,1)$ or $g_0 \in \gp{K}$.
nodes.statement_short: Translation preserves $\intL^1$-ness and kills the residual part when $\Reis \in \Reis^+$ or $g_0 \in \gp{K}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: $R(s, \eis^{(n_1)}(0,f_1) \eis^{(n_2)}(0,f_2))$ resp. $R(s, \eis^{\sharp,(n_1)}(1/2,f_1) \eis^{\sharp,(n_2)}(1/2,f_2))$ represents the value at $s_1=s_2=0$ of $\partial_1^{n_1} \partial_2^{n_2}$ of $$ \Lambda(1/2+s+s_1+s_2, \xi_1\xi_2) \Lambda(1/2+s+s_1-s_2, \xi_1\xi_2') \Lambda(1/2+s-s_1+s_2, \xi_1'\xi_2) \Lambda(1/2+s-s_1-s_2, \xi_1'\xi_2') \quad \text{resp.} $$ $$ \Lambda(3/2+s+s_1+s_2, \xi_1\xi_2) \Lambda(1/2+s+s_1-s_2, \xi_1\xi_2') \Lambda(1/2+s-s_1+s_2, \xi_1'\xi_2) \Lambda(-1/2+s-s_1-s_2, \xi_1'\xi_2'), $$ which is regular at $s=1/2$ by assumption. The degenerate part is also easily seen to be $0$ by assumption. We conclude by Definition \ref{RegIntDef}.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $R(s,\cdot)$ with a product of four $\Lambda$-functions, regular at $s=1/2$ under the hypothesis, and note the degenerate part vanishes.

nodes.name: Express $R(s,\cdot)$ as a product of four completed $L$-functions
nodes.statement: $R(s, \eis^{(n_1)}(0,f_1) \eis^{(n_2)}(0,f_2))$ resp. $R(s, \eis^{\sharp,(n_1)}(1/2,f_1) \eis^{\sharp,(n_2)}(1/2,f_2))$ represents the value at $s_1=s_2=0$ of $\partial_1^{n_1} \partial_2^{n_2}$ of $$ \Lambda(1/2+s+s_1+s_2, \xi_1\xi_2) \Lambda(1/2+s+s_1-s_2, \xi_1\xi_2') \Lambda(1/2+s-s_1+s_2, \xi_1'\xi_2) \Lambda(1/2+s-s_1-s_2, \xi_1'\xi_2') \quad \text{resp.} $$ $$ \Lambda(3/2+s+s_1+s_2, \xi_1\xi_2) \Lambda(1/2+s+s_1-s_2, \xi_1\xi_2') \Lambda(1/2+s-s_1+s_2, \xi_1'\xi_2) \Lambda(-1/2+s-s_1-s_2, \xi_1'\xi_2'), $$ which is regular at $s=1/2$ by assumption.
nodes.statement_short: The Rankin-Selberg integral is a derivative of a fourfold $\Lambda$-product, regular at $s=1/2$.

nodes.name: The degenerate part vanishes
nodes.statement: The degenerate part is also easily seen to be $0$ by assumption. We conclude by Definition \ref{RegIntDef}.
nodes.statement_short: The degenerate contribution is zero under the same hypothesis.

nodes.name: Conclude from the definition of the regularized integral
nodes.statement: We conclude by Definition \ref{RegIntDef}.
nodes.statement_short: No residue and no degenerate term, hence the integral vanishes.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement: This is a variant of Lemma \ref{SimpleProd}.
nodes.statement_short: A variant of the regular-case vanishing Lemma 3.1.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: The first formula follows immediately from Proposition \ref{RegGInv} and definition. The second one is a variant of Lemma \ref{SimpleProd}.
nodes.statement_short: First formula from Proposition 2.26 and the definition; second formula as a variant of Lemma 3.1.

nodes.name: First formula from Proposition 2.26
nodes.statement: The first formula follows immediately from Proposition \ref{RegGInv} and definition.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the vanishing of the regularized integral on the residual space.

nodes.name: Second formula as a variant of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: The second one is a variant of Lemma \ref{SimpleProd}.
nodes.statement_short: Same $L$-function argument as in the regular case.

nodes.name: Derivation of Theorem 3.4 (2) by deformation
nodes.statement: We continue to use the notations in the previous lemma. We can write $$ \eisCst(s,f_1) \eisCst^{(1)}(0,f_2) = 2(f_1f_2)_{1/2+s}^{(1)} + 2(\Intw_s f_1f_2)_{1/2-s}^{(1)} + (f_1 \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2)_{1/2+s} + (\Intw_s f_1 \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2)_{1/2-s}. $$ We tentatively define \begin{align*} \Reis^{\reg}(s) &:= s^{-1} \left\{ 2 \eis^{\reg,(1)}(1/2+s, f_1f_2) + 2 \eis^{\reg,(1)}(1/2-s, \Intw_s f_1f_2) \right. \\ &\left. + \eis^{\reg}(1/2+s, f_1 \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2) + \eis^{\reg}(1/2-s, \Intw_s f_1 \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2) \right\} \end{align*} Applying Lemma \ref{SimpleProdU}, \ref{SimpleProdSing} with $n=0, 1$ together with (\ref{DeformTec}), we get \begin{align*} \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \eis^{(1)}(0,f_1) \eis^{(1)}(0,f_2) &= \lim_{s \to 0} \int_{[\PGL_2]} s^{-1} \eis(s,f_1) \eis^{(1)}(0,f_2) - \Reis^{\reg}(s) \\ &= \frac{1}{s} \cdot \left\{ 2 \frac{\lambda_{\F}^{(1)}(s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1f_2) + 2 \frac{\lambda_{\F}^{(1)}(-s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(\Intw_s f_1f_2) \right. \\ &\left. + \frac{\lambda_{\F}(s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1 \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2) + \frac{\lambda_{\F}(-s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(\Intw_s f_1 \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2) \right\}. \end{align*} Taking Laurent expansions, we verify that the function in $s$ in the range of the above limit is regular at $s=0$, unlike its appearance. The properties $$ \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1 \Intw_0^{(k)}f_2) = \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_2 \Intw_0^{(k)}f_1), \forall k \in \ag{N}; \quad \Intw_0^{(2)} = \Intw_0^{(1)} \circ \Intw_0^{(1)} $$ $$ \text{coming from} \quad \Intw_s \circ \Intw_{-s} = 1 $$ must be used. Taking limit as $s \to 0$, we obtain (2) of the following:
nodes.statement_short: Deformation argument: expand the constant term of $\eis(s,f_1)\eis^{(1)}(0,f_2)$, subtract a tentative residual family $\Reis^{\reg}(s)$, apply the vanishing lemmas and let $s \to 0$.

nodes.name: Expand the constant term of the deformed product
nodes.statement: We continue to use the notations in the previous lemma. We can write $$ \eisCst(s,f_1) \eisCst^{(1)}(0,f_2) = 2(f_1f_2)_{1/2+s}^{(1)} + 2(\Intw_s f_1f_2)_{1/2-s}^{(1)} + (f_1 \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2)_{1/2+s} + (\Intw_s f_1 \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2)_{1/2-s}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Write $\eisCst(s,f_1)\eisCst^{(1)}(0,f_2)$ as four flat-section terms.

nodes.name: Define the tentative residual family $\Reis^{\reg}(s)$
nodes.statement: We tentatively define \begin{align*} \Reis^{\reg}(s) &:= s^{-1} \left\{ 2 \eis^{\reg,(1)}(1/2+s, f_1f_2) + 2 \eis^{\reg,(1)}(1/2-s, \Intw_s f_1f_2) \right. \\ &\left. + \eis^{\reg}(1/2+s, f_1 \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2) + \eis^{\reg}(1/2-s, \Intw_s f_1 \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2) \right\} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Assemble the matching residual family with an $s^{-1}$ normalization.

nodes.name: Apply the vanishing lemmas and the deformation identity
nodes.statement: Applying Lemma \ref{SimpleProdU}, \ref{SimpleProdSing} with $n=0, 1$ together with (\ref{DeformTec}), we get \begin{align*} \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \eis^{(1)}(0,f_1) \eis^{(1)}(0,f_2) &= \lim_{s \to 0} \int_{[\PGL_2]} s^{-1} \eis(s,f_1) \eis^{(1)}(0,f_2) - \Reis^{\reg}(s) \\ &= \frac{1}{s} \cdot \left\{ 2 \frac{\lambda_{\F}^{(1)}(s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1f_2) + 2 \frac{\lambda_{\F}^{(1)}(-s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(\Intw_s f_1f_2) \right. \\ &\left. + \frac{\lambda_{\F}(s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1 \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2) + \frac{\lambda_{\F}(-s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(\Intw_s f_1 \Intw_0^{(1)}f_2) \right\}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 3.3 and 3.6 with the deformation principle give the limit as an explicit $\lambda_{\F}$-expression.

nodes.name: Check regularity at $s=0$ and pass to the limit
nodes.statement: Taking Laurent expansions, we verify that the function in $s$ in the range of the above limit is regular at $s=0$, unlike its appearance. The properties $$ \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1 \Intw_0^{(k)}f_2) = \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_2 \Intw_0^{(k)}f_1), \forall k \in \ag{N}; \quad \Intw_0^{(2)} = \Intw_0^{(1)} \circ \Intw_0^{(1)} $$ $$ \text{coming from} \quad \Intw_s \circ \Intw_{-s} = 1 $$ must be used. Taking limit as $s \to 0$, we obtain (2) of the following:
nodes.statement_short: Laurent expansion plus the symmetry of $\ProjP_{\gp{K}}$ and $\Intw_0^{(2)}=(\Intw_0^{(1)})^2$ give the limit.

nodes.name: Derivation of Theorem 3.7 (3) by deformation
nodes.statement: We continue to use the notations in the previous section and lemma. Denote $e=e_1$. We can write $$ \eisCst^{\reg}(s,f) = f_s + (\widetilde{\Intw}_s f)_{-s} + \lambda_{\F}(s-\frac{1}{2}) \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f) \left( e_{-s} - e_{-1/2} \right); $$ \begin{align*} \eisCst^{\reg,(n)}(\frac{1}{2},f) &= f_{1/2}^{(n)} + \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} (-1)^k (\widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2}^{(n-k)} f)_{-1/2}^{(k)} \\ &+ \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f) \cdot \left\{ \frac{(-1)^{n+1} \lambda_{\F}^{-1)}(0)}{n+1} e_{-1/2}^{(n+1)} + \sum_{k=1}^n \binom{n}{k} (-1)^k \lambda_{\F}^{(n-k)}(0) e_{-1/2}^k \right\}, \end{align*} from which one easily deduce $\eisCst^{\reg}(1/2+s,f_1) \eisCst^{\reg,(n_2)}(1/2,f_2)$. We tentatively define \begin{align*} \Reis^{\reg}(s) &:= \eis^{(n_2)}(\frac{3}{2}+s, f_1f_2) + \sum_{k=0}^{n_2} \binom{n_2}{k} (-1)^k \eis^{\reg, (k)}(\frac{1}{2}+s, f_1 \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2}^{(n_2-k)} f_2) \\ &\quad + \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_2) \cdot \left\{ \frac{(-1)^{n_2+1} \lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)}{n_2+1} \eis^{\reg,(n_2+1)}(\frac{1}{2}+s, f_1) \right. \\ &\quad \left. + \sum_{k=1}^{n_2} \binom{n_2}{k} (-1)^k \lambda_{\F}^{(n_2-k)}(0) \eis^{\reg,(k)}(\frac{1}{2}+s, f_1) \right\} \\ &\quad + \eis^{\reg,(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2}-s, f_2 \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2+s}f_1) \\ &\quad + \lambda_{\F}(s) \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1) \cdot \left\{ \eis^{\reg,(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2}-s, f_2) - \eis^{\reg,(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2}, f_2) \right\}. \end{align*} Applying Lemma \ref{SimpleProdSing} with $n_1=0$ together with (\ref{DeformTec}), we get \begin{align*} &\quad \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \eis^{\reg}(\frac{1}{2},f_1) \eis^{\reg,(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2},f_2) = \lim_{s \to 0} \int_{[\PGL_2]} \eis^{\reg}(\frac{1}{2}+s,f_1) \eis^{\reg,(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2},f_2) - \Reis^{\reg}(s) \\ &= \lim_{s \to 0} \sum_{k=0}^{n_2} \binom{n_2}{k} \frac{(-1)^k}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \lambda_{\F}^{(k)}(s) \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1 \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2}^{(n_2-k)} f_2) + \frac{\lambda_{\F}^{(n_2)}(-s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_2 \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2+s}f_1) \\ &\quad + \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1) \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_2) \cdot \left\{ \frac{(-1)^{n_2+1} \lambda_{\F}^{(n_2+1)}(s)}{n_2+1} + \sum_{k=1}^{n_2} \binom{n_2}{k} (-1)^k \frac{\lambda_{\F}^{(n_2-k)}(0) \lambda_{\F}^{(k)}(s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} + \lambda_{\F}(s) \lambda_{\F}^{(n_2)}(-s) \right\}. \end{align*} Taking Laurent expansions, we verify that the function in $s$ in the range of the above limit is regular at $s=0$, unlike its appearance. The symmetry $$ \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1 \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2}^{(k)}f_2) = \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_2 \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2}^{(k)}f_1), \forall k \in \ag{N} $$ must be used. Moreover, it can be differentiated $n_1$ times to deduce (3) of the following:
nodes.statement_short: Same deformation scheme in the singular case: expand $\eisCst^{\reg}$ and its derivatives, subtract the tentative $\Reis^{\reg}(s)$, apply Lemma 3.6 and differentiate $n_1$ times.

nodes.name: Expand the constant terms of the regularizing Eisenstein series
nodes.statement: We continue to use the notations in the previous section and lemma. Denote $e=e_1$. We can write $$ \eisCst^{\reg}(s,f) = f_s + (\widetilde{\Intw}_s f)_{-s} + \lambda_{\F}(s-\frac{1}{2}) \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f) \left( e_{-s} - e_{-1/2} \right); $$ \begin{align*} \eisCst^{\reg,(n)}(\frac{1}{2},f) &= f_{1/2}^{(n)} + \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k} (-1)^k (\widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2}^{(n-k)} f)_{-1/2}^{(k)} \\ &+ \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f) \cdot \left\{ \frac{(-1)^{n+1} \lambda_{\F}^{-1)}(0)}{n+1} e_{-1/2}^{(n+1)} + \sum_{k=1}^n \binom{n}{k} (-1)^k \lambda_{\F}^{(n-k)}(0) e_{-1/2}^k \right\}, \end{align*} from which one easily deduce $\eisCst^{\reg}(1/2+s,f_1) \eisCst^{\reg,(n_2)}(1/2,f_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\eisCst^{\reg}(s,f)$ and its $n$-th derivative at $1/2$ explicitly.

nodes.name: Define the tentative residual family $\Reis^{\reg}(s)$
nodes.statement: We tentatively define \begin{align*} \Reis^{\reg}(s) &:= \eis^{(n_2)}(\frac{3}{2}+s, f_1f_2) + \sum_{k=0}^{n_2} \binom{n_2}{k} (-1)^k \eis^{\reg, (k)}(\frac{1}{2}+s, f_1 \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2}^{(n_2-k)} f_2) \\ &\quad + \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_2) \cdot \left\{ \frac{(-1)^{n_2+1} \lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)}{n_2+1} \eis^{\reg,(n_2+1)}(\frac{1}{2}+s, f_1) \right. \\ &\quad \left. + \sum_{k=1}^{n_2} \binom{n_2}{k} (-1)^k \lambda_{\F}^{(n_2-k)}(0) \eis^{\reg,(k)}(\frac{1}{2}+s, f_1) \right\} \\ &\quad + \eis^{\reg,(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2}-s, f_2 \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2+s}f_1) \\ &\quad + \lambda_{\F}(s) \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1) \cdot \left\{ \eis^{\reg,(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2}-s, f_2) - \eis^{\reg,(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2}, f_2) \right\}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Assemble the residual family matching every term of the expanded constant term.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3.6 and the deformation identity
nodes.statement: Applying Lemma \ref{SimpleProdSing} with $n_1=0$ together with (\ref{DeformTec}), we get \begin{align*} &\quad \int_{[\PGL_2]}^{\reg} \eis^{\reg}(\frac{1}{2},f_1) \eis^{\reg,(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2},f_2) = \lim_{s \to 0} \int_{[\PGL_2]} \eis^{\reg}(\frac{1}{2}+s,f_1) \eis^{\reg,(n_2)}(\frac{1}{2},f_2) - \Reis^{\reg}(s) \\ &= \lim_{s \to 0} \sum_{k=0}^{n_2} \binom{n_2}{k} \frac{(-1)^k}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \lambda_{\F}^{(k)}(s) \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1 \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2}^{(n_2-k)} f_2) + \frac{\lambda_{\F}^{(n_2)}(-s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_2 \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2+s}f_1) \\ &\quad + \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1) \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_2) \cdot \left\{ \frac{(-1)^{n_2+1} \lambda_{\F}^{(n_2+1)}(s)}{n_2+1} + \sum_{k=1}^{n_2} \binom{n_2}{k} (-1)^k \frac{\lambda_{\F}^{(n_2-k)}(0) \lambda_{\F}^{(k)}(s)}{\lambda_{\F}^{(-1)}(0)} + \lambda_{\F}(s) \lambda_{\F}^{(n_2)}(-s) \right\}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The limit becomes an explicit combination of $\lambda_{\F}$-derivatives and $\ProjP_{\gp{K}}$-terms.

nodes.name: Check regularity at $s=0$ and differentiate $n_1$ times
nodes.statement: Taking Laurent expansions, we verify that the function in $s$ in the range of the above limit is regular at $s=0$, unlike its appearance. The symmetry $$ \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1 \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2}^{(k)}f_2) = \ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_2 \widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2}^{(k)}f_1), \forall k \in \ag{N} $$ must be used. Moreover, it can be differentiated $n_1$ times to deduce (3) of the following:
nodes.statement_short: Using the symmetry of $\ProjP_{\gp{K}}(f_1\widetilde{\Intw}_{1/2}^{(k)}f_2)$, differentiate to get part (3).

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.13
nodes.statement: By integration by parts we get $$ \Mellin{f}(s) = \frac{(-1)^k}{s(s+1) \cdots (s+k-1)} \int_0^{\infty} f^{(k)}(y) y^{s+k} \frac{dy}{y}, $$ from which it follows readily that $H_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(\Mellin{f}) \leq B_1^{k,\sigma}(f)$. Similarly we pass the derivatives under the integral to get $$ f_M^{(k)}(y) = (-1)^k \int_{\Re s = \sigma} s(s+1) \cdots (s+k-1) M(s)y^{-s-k} \frac{ds}{2\pi i}, $$ from which it follows readily that $B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(f_M) \leq H_1^{k,\sigma}(M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Integration by parts for the Mellin transform and differentiation under the integral for its inverse give $H_{\infty}^{k,\sigma} \leq B_1^{k,\sigma}$ and $B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma} \leq H_1^{k,\sigma}$.

nodes.name: Integration by parts for the Mellin transform
nodes.statement: By integration by parts we get $$ \Mellin{f}(s) = \frac{(-1)^k}{s(s+1) \cdots (s+k-1)} \int_0^{\infty} f^{(k)}(y) y^{s+k} \frac{dy}{y}, $$ from which it follows readily that $H_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(\Mellin{f}) \leq B_1^{k,\sigma}(f)$.
nodes.statement_short: $k$-fold integration by parts yields $H_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(\Mellin{f}) \leq B_1^{k,\sigma}(f)$.

nodes.name: Differentiate the inverse transform under the integral
nodes.statement: Similarly we pass the derivatives under the integral to get $$ f_M^{(k)}(y) = (-1)^k \int_{\Re s = \sigma} s(s+1) \cdots (s+k-1) M(s)y^{-s-k} \frac{ds}{2\pi i}, $$ from which it follows readily that $B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(f_M) \leq H_1^{k,\sigma}(M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Differentiating gives $B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(f_M) \leq H_1^{k,\sigma}(M)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.15
nodes.statement: In the case $\F=\ag{R}$, we have $$ t^k\frac{d^k}{dt^k} f(t;+) = \frac{1}{2} \left( t^kf^{(k)}(t) + (-1)^k t^k f^{(k)}(-t) \right), $$ $$ t^k\frac{d^k}{dt^k} f(t;-) = \frac{1}{2} \left( t^kf^{(k)}(t) + (-1)^{k+1} t^k f^{(k)}(-t) \right), $$ from which it is easy to see $$ B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(f_{\pm}) \leq \Sch_{\infty}^{\lfloor k+\sigma \rfloor, k}(f) + \Sch_{\infty}^{\lceil k+\sigma \rceil, k}(f), \forall k \in \ag{N}, \sigma > 0. $$ In the case $\F=\ag{C}$, with the Cartesian \& Polar coordinates $$ (x,y) = (t \cos \theta, t \sin \theta), (z,\bar{z})=(x+iy,x-iy) $$ we have $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} = i \left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right); t\frac{\partial}{\partial t} = z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}}. $$ By induction on $k \in \ag{N}$, it is easy to see $$ t^k \frac{\partial^k}{\partial t^k} = P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}}) $$ for some polynomial $P_k \in \ag{Z}[X]$ and any $k \in \ag{N}$. It follows that \begin{align*} t^k f_n^{(k)}(t) &= \int_{\ag{R} / 2\pi \ag{Z}} (P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}})f)(te^{i\theta}) e^{in\theta} \frac{d\theta}{2\pi} \\ &= \frac{(-1)^l}{n^l} \int_{\ag{R} / 2\pi \ag{Z}} (\left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right)^l P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}})f)(te^{i\theta}) e^{in\theta} \frac{d\theta}{2\pi}. \end{align*} Hence, we deduce that \begin{align*} B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(f_n) &\leq \norm[n]^{-l} \left\{ \extNorm{(z\bar{z})^{\lfloor \frac{\sigma}{2} \rfloor}\left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right)^l P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}})f}_{\infty} \right. \\ &\quad \left. + \extNorm{(z\bar{z})^{\lceil \frac{\sigma}{2} \rceil}\left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right)^l P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}})f}_{\infty} \right\}. \end{align*} The right hand side is obviously bounded by some Schwartz norm of $f$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation for $\F=\ag{R}$; for $\F=\ag{C}$ convert $t\partial_t$ and $\partial_{\theta}$ into $z\partial_z \pm \bar{z}\partial_{\bar{z}}$, integrate by parts in $\theta$ to gain $n^{-l}$.

nodes.name: Case $\F = \ag{R}$
nodes.statement: In the case $\F=\ag{R}$, we have $$ t^k\frac{d^k}{dt^k} f(t;+) = \frac{1}{2} \left( t^kf^{(k)}(t) + (-1)^k t^k f^{(k)}(-t) \right), $$ $$ t^k\frac{d^k}{dt^k} f(t;-) = \frac{1}{2} \left( t^kf^{(k)}(t) + (-1)^{k+1} t^k f^{(k)}(-t) \right), $$ from which it is easy to see $$ B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(f_{\pm}) \leq \Sch_{\infty}^{\lfloor k+\sigma \rfloor, k}(f) + \Sch_{\infty}^{\lceil k+\sigma \rceil, k}(f), \forall k \in \ag{N}, \sigma > 0. $$
nodes.statement_short: The even and odd parts have derivatives bounded by two Schwartz norms.

nodes.name: Case $\F = \ag{C}$: polar versus Cartesian derivations
nodes.statement: In the case $\F=\ag{C}$, with the Cartesian \& Polar coordinates $$ (x,y) = (t \cos \theta, t \sin \theta), (z,\bar{z})=(x+iy,x-iy) $$ we have $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} = i \left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right); t\frac{\partial}{\partial t} = z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Express $\partial_{\theta}$ and $t\partial_t$ through $z\partial_z$ and $\bar{z}\partial_{\bar{z}}$.

nodes.name: Induct on $k$ and integrate by parts in $\theta$
nodes.statement: By induction on $k \in \ag{N}$, it is easy to see $$ t^k \frac{\partial^k}{\partial t^k} = P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}}) $$ for some polynomial $P_k \in \ag{Z}[X]$ and any $k \in \ag{N}$. It follows that \begin{align*} t^k f_n^{(k)}(t) &= \int_{\ag{R} / 2\pi \ag{Z}} (P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}})f)(te^{i\theta}) e^{in\theta} \frac{d\theta}{2\pi} \\ &= \frac{(-1)^l}{n^l} \int_{\ag{R} / 2\pi \ag{Z}} (\left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right)^l P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}})f)(te^{i\theta}) e^{in\theta} \frac{d\theta}{2\pi}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $t^k\partial_t^k$ is a polynomial in $z\partial_z+\bar{z}\partial_{\bar{z}}$; $l$ integrations by parts produce $n^{-l}$.

nodes.name: Bound by Schwartz norms
nodes.statement: Hence, we deduce that \begin{align*} B_{\infty}^{k,\sigma}(f_n) &\leq \norm[n]^{-l} \left\{ \extNorm{(z\bar{z})^{\lfloor \frac{\sigma}{2} \rfloor}\left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right)^l P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}})f}_{\infty} \right. \\ &\quad \left. + \extNorm{(z\bar{z})^{\lceil \frac{\sigma}{2} \rceil}\left( z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} - \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}} \right)^l P_k(z \frac{\partial}{\partial z} + \bar{z} \frac{\partial}{\partial \bar{z}})f}_{\infty} \right\}. \end{align*} The right hand side is obviously bounded by some Schwartz norm of $f$.
nodes.statement_short: The resulting sup-norms are Schwartz norms of $f$.

Writing $$ f(y) = \int_{\ag{C}^{\times}} \Phi(t,\frac{y}{t}) \omega^{-1}\xi^2(t)\norm[t]_{\ag{C}}^{2s} d^{\times}t, $$ we can take its Fourier expansion on $\ag{C}^1$ $$ f(te^{i\theta}) = \sum_{n \in \ag{Z}} f_n(t) e^{-in\theta}, t \in \ag{R}_+. $$

Hence $f_n \in \fsB_{\max(0,-4\Re s)}(\ag{R}_+)$ and for any $\sigma > \max(0,-4\Re s)$ we get $$ \norm[t^{\sigma}f(te^{i\theta})] \leq \sum_n B_{\infty}^{0,\sigma}(f_n) \ll \Sch_1^*(\Phi) \sum_n \min(1, \norm[n]^{-2}). $$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.19
nodes.statement_short: Average over a ball of additive invariance for the sup bound, integrate over the support for the $\intL^l$ bound, and bound $\norm[x]^{\sigma}$ on the support for the last.

nodes.name: Sup norm bounded by the $\intL^l$ norm
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove the case $d=1$. Let $x_0 \in \F$ be such that $\norm[\Phi(x_0)] = \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}$, then $$ \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l = \Vol(\vp^{\delta(\Phi)})^{-1} \int_{x_0 + \vp^{\delta(\Phi)}} \norm[\Phi(x)]^l dx \leq q^{\delta(\Phi)} \Norm[\Phi]_l^l $$ and we get the first inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Average $|\Phi|^l$ over a ball of invariance around a maximum point.

nodes.name: $\intL^l$ norm bounded by the sup norm
nodes.statement: The second follows from $$ \Norm[\Phi]_l^l \leq \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l \int_{{\rm supp}(\Phi)} dx \leq \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l \cdot \Vol(\vp^{D(\Phi)}) = q^{-D(\Phi)} \Norm[\Phi]_{\infty}^l. $$
nodes.statement_short: Integrate the sup bound over the support of volume $q^{-D(\Phi)}$.
